items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1959-10-26
items.q: Aided in a better by no other than Dr. Sushant, who puts himself as a jazz historian... But up to that time Dr. Sushon was with me.

ctx.x: Maybe I'll get in trouble by mentioning Edgar Stein but he put money in there. But this Edgar Stein had a lot to do from keeping me from getting recognition because he was a big owner in the times, picking on a long time ago. And I found out all this stuff, not recently, but in a roundabout way, things have been rounding themselves up. this Dave Stein came here, he bought the New Orleans item in. He was the same man who created the talking mule, Francis. He helped to create the talking jackasses, the New Orleans…

Aided in a better by no other than Dr. Sushant, who puts himself as a jazz historian. Now this man here, as a jazz historian, never played jazz. He says he used to sit across the road from on Basin Street and listen to Joe Oliver playing music. And there's where he got his idea from. Well now the only thing he could have heard on Basin Street, and there's many more men as old as I am, can tell you they had no music on Basin Street outside a little violin or a piano. Or they had three Negro Rhymers at Anderson's.…

items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-06-16
items.q: He came down to New Orleans and he sold them a bill of goods to Myra Menville and Dr. Sushant.

ctx.x: You don't see anything in front of me that I take notes from, only just from what comes to my mind. That's why I don't have it in chronological order. I can only tell you what I can think of at the time. Maybe my talk may be gobbled up a little bit, that I might put this one before the other one, the other one before the other one. But I am telling you the true facts of this music. It was in Chicago where I changed the rhythm. They had a certain dance team. They were doing a castle walk. And up in the north,…
Can you hold it a second?

items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1959-06-14
items.q: I've been told that he's been back here under Dr. Sushant's wing to make a tape recording on jazz.

ctx.x: And they're saying there was some part of the creation of jazz. That Jack Lane, who played a drum and lousy drums at that, created jazz. Now that's good enough for men who thrive on thievery, on a word that we had nothing to do. Our jazz was started in Chicago. We took in the ragtime and changed the rhythm in Chicago. In 1916, we seen we were going to be a flop the first night. And I, being a good dancer, I watched those people. At that time, they had Vernon Castle doing the castle walk. And everybody was trying…

No, I wrote that mostly as a sort of, you might say, editor. Walter Allen managed to interview the various musicians that were still living. And he sent me the facts and I wrote them, sewed them up together. I was more concerned with the records than with the legends. I wasn't very interested in these obscure people from the shadows who were said to have played with this, that and the other musician, in this, that and the other band, and who never made any records at all. I'm not interested in music I can't hear…
